extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, regulators, employers, employment lawyers, and public commenters on the FTC non-compete rule
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and evidentiary standards the FTC uses to assess whether non-compete clauses with non-senior-executive workers constitute an unfair method of competition under Section 5, including how empirical studies and comment evidence are weighed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer direct measures or effective proxies in empirical studies
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission gives more weight to studies that measure the exact outcome of interest or studies that use effective proxies; weak or inapt proxies (e.g., patent counts alone) are generally less persuasive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a study that analyzes non-compete enforceability using number of patents issued is a weaker proxy for innovation than a study that also measures patent quality. The Commission prefers studies that directly measure the outcome or use robust proxies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holistic expert assessment of empirical evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond guiding principles, the Commission's assessment of empirical studies is holistic and relies on its economic expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission considers characteristics important in any context, such as data quality, statistical precision, and other factors when weighing studies; not a mechanical checklist but an expert, overall judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 5 two-element inquiry (method of competition and unfairness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under section 5 the Commission assesses (1) whether the conduct is a method of competition (specific conduct by an actor) versus a condition of the marketplace, and (2) whether the conduct is unfair—meaning it goes beyond competition on the merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both elements must be evaluated; 'method of competition' focuses on specific conduct; 'unfair' includes indicia of unfairness and tendency to negatively affect competitive conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unfairness inquiry components: indicia and tendency
rubrics_metrics.description: The unfairness inquiry has two components: (a) whether the conduct has indicia of unfairness, and (b) whether the conduct tends to negatively affect competitive conditions; these are weighed on a sliding scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stronger indicia of unfairness can require less proof of tendency, and vice versa. The Commission may rely more heavily on indicia (e.g., exploitative conduct) in some contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency standard (no need for case-specific proven harm)
rubrics_metrics.description: The legal standard requires only a tendency to negatively affect competitive conditions; it does not turn on whether the conduct directly caused actual harm in a specific instance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission finds that a tendency can be inferred from the nature and function of the conduct and supported by empirical evidence and comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct vs marketplace condition: non-competes are a method of competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-competes are specific conduct undertaken by an actor in a marketplace—not merely a condition of the marketplace—and thus qualify as a method of competition under section 5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No commenters disputed this finding; non-competes are treated as actor conduct subject to scrutiny, not as a neutral market condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictive conduct indicium
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicia of unfairness are present where conduct is restrictive: non-competes restrict a worker's ability to seek or accept other work or start a business and restrict competitors from hiring that worker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission treats restrictive conduct as including both restriction and exclusion; restrictions that force workers out of the labor market or prevent reasonable alternatives weigh heavily in the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusionary conduct indicium
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-competes are exclusionary where they tend to impair the opportunities of rivals—by limiting rival firms' ability to hire workers, impairing firms' ability to expand into markets, or deterring entrepreneurs from starting businesses in the market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusionary effects are considered separately from restriction; widespread non-compete use that impairs entry or hiring supports a finding of exclusionary conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploitative/coercive conduct indicium
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct may violate section 5 where it is exploitative or coercive and tends to negatively affect competitive conditions; non-competes are exploitative/coercive if employers take advantage of unequal bargaining power to impose them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploitative/coercive indicators include unilateral imposition, lack of negotiation or compensation, and forcing workers to stay or bear significant harms or costs at departure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unilateral imposition as evidence of exploitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers almost always unilaterally impose non-competes, exploiting superior bargaining power to impose significant restrictions without meaningful negotiation or compensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence includes standard-form contracts, non-competes presented post-offer or on first day of work, workers rarely bargaining or seeking counsel, and reports of non-negotiability even where counsel is available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation timing and concealment increase coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-competes presented after a job offer, on the first day of work, after a merger/acquisition, or hidden/obscured in paperwork increase coercion and reduce workers' ability to negotiate or refuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from comments: non-competes buried in onboarding packets, provided with one business day to review, or added in later share agreements—practices that diminish meaningful consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of counsel as indicium of unequal bargaining power
rubrics_metrics.description: Most workers do not seek assistance of counsel when entering non-competes—evidence that workers lack the resources or bargaining power to negotiate or understand restrictive covenants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission cites research (Starr, Prescott, & Bishara) finding less than 8% of workers seek counsel; this supports the conclusion that many non-competes are imposed without meaningful legal advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: In terrorem / chilling effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-competes exert a powerful in terrorem effect: they trap workers in jobs and deter competitive activity even when workers believe the non-competes are overbroad or unenforceable, because litigation threats are financially and reputationally intimidating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission treats the chilling effect—fear of litigation, attorneys' fees, arbitration clauses, or reputational harm—as a form of coercion relevant to unfairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harms and costs that demonstrate coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-competes coerce when they force workers to stay in unwanted jobs or to bear significant harms/costs such as leaving the workforce, relocating, enduring long commutes, or facing expensive litigation risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenter anecdotes describing relocation, family disruption, long commutes, lost earnings, and inability to work in one's field are used as evidence of these harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employers' labor market power factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission considers factors that give employers labor market power—industry/location concentration, information asymmetries, limited worker mobility, outsourcing/misclassification, wage-sharing/fixing, and use of NDAs or mandatory arbitration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These structural and behavioral factors support findings that employers can exploit workers and that non-competes can be coercive/exploitative even in markets without high concentration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of unenforceable non-competes still indicative of coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers frequently use non-competes even when they are unenforceable under State law; that usage (and reminders of non-competes on departure) can deter workers and competitors regardless of formal enforceability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons include employer expectation of law changes, forum shopping, reliance on workers' lack of legal knowledge, and the chilling effect of potential litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court modification risk increases chilling effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Even overbroad non-competes can chill behavior because courts may modify or 'blue-pencil' provisions rather than invalidate them; this possibility increases workers' litigation risk and deterrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission notes that modification doctrines or partial enforcement mean overbroad drafting can still lead to enforcement costs and deterrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special vulnerabilities amplify coercive effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain worker characteristics—state licensing requirements, specialized skillsets with narrow geographic or industry demand, high student loan debt, or other mobility constraints—heighten the coercive impact of non-competes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: physicians with state licenses, dentists with student debt, niche technical roles with few alternative employers; these factors make relocation or career changes more costly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation and severance practices relevant to coercion assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether workers receive compensation for signing non-competes (e.g., severance conditioned on signing) and whether such compensation is meaningful or actually paid are relevant to whether a covenant is exploitative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission cites examples where severance was tied to non-competes, buyout fees were demanded, or promised compensation was withheld—practices that may indicate coercion rather than fair bargaining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractual clauses that deter challenges (attorneys' fees, arbitration, clawbacks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clauses such as attorneys' fee-shifting, forced arbitration, and compensation clawbacks increase the cost and difficulty of challenging non-competes and thus are relevant indicia of coercion and deterrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of these provisions in non-competes or related contracts supports the conclusion that employers can intimidate workers from exercising mobility or challenging covenants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Less-restrictive-alternative consideration (trade secret law)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission considers whether less-restrictive alternatives (e.g., trade secret law) can protect legitimate employer interests without the restrictive effects of non-competes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission points to Part IV.D.2 for analysis comparing non-competes to alternatives like trade secret protection, implying non-competes may be unnecessary where narrower tools suffice.
